extracted.intended_audience: judges and patent litigators preparing jury instructions and trial counsel in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials covering invalidity defenses (anticipation, prior invention, prior patent/application), obviousness (Graham factors), enablement, written description, and damages — intended to guide courts and counsel in framing jury questions and legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / anticipation — enabling disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed publication (including an issued patent or a published patent application as of its publication date) is a printed publication as prior art only if the disclosure of the claimed invention in the printed publication is complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to use the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining whether the disclosure is enabling, consider what would have been within the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date, and you may consider evidence that sheds light on the knowledge such a person would have had.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — proof standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if a third party invented the claimed invention in the United States before the patentee invented it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [The Defendant] must show it is highly probable that (1) before [the patentee] invented his invention, [third party] reduced to practice a [product/method] that included all of the features of the claim, or (2) [third party] was first to conceive the invention and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. Additionally, [third party]'s product/method must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized that it would work for its intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment (prior invention defense negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior invention does not anticipate if it was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed by the prior inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may find abandonment, suppression, or concealment if it is highly probable the prior inventor actively concealed the invention from the public or unreasonably delayed making it publicly known. Generally, a prior invention was not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed if the invention was made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used for a commercial purpose. A period of delay does not constitute abandonment if the prior inventor engaged in reasonable efforts to bring the prior invention to market during the delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (pre-AIA) as invalidating prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country by another before the patentee invented it (or, where applicable, more than one year before the patentee filed the U.S. patent application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual dispute about the date of invention or priority date, the jury should be instructed on how to determine the date of invention; otherwise the Court should instruct the jury as to the Cutoff Date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (AIA) — effective filing date standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the claimed invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual disputes exist about whether a disclosure in a patent resulted from the inventor/joint inventor or from another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor, the jury should be instructed on exceptions under § 102(b)(1) as needed. The instruction must identify the claimed invention's effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior U.S. application / published patent document (pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application, PCT published in English, or U.S. patent filed/published by another before the relevant invention date or effective filing date (depending on pre-AIA/AIA rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the published application was effectively filed under 35 U.S.C. § 102(d) (AIA) and whether disclosure was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor, publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor, or owned by the same person — instruct the jury on exceptions under §§ 102(b)(2) and (c) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is invalid as obvious if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Obviousness may be shown by one or more items of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hindsight; do not use the patent as a road map for selecting and combining prior art. The defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Perform a separate analysis for each asserted claim. The following four Graham factors must be evaluated (scope/content of prior art; differences; level of ordinary skill; additional considerations), though in any order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor 1 — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the prior art references to be considered and determine their scope and content as received into evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem or need addressed by the patent, or if it discloses information with obvious uses beyond its main purpose that a person of ordinary skill would reasonably examine when solving the patent's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor 2 — differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date; determine the impact of those differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inferences and creative steps a POSA would employ. Combination of known elements yielding predictable results favors obviousness; unexpected or unpredictable results, or references teaching away, favor nonobviousness. A claim is not obvious merely because each element was independently known. If inherency is alleged to supply a missing element, it may be used only if the element is the natural result of the explicit prior art combination and not established by mere probabilities or possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor 3 — level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the Cutoff Date; this factor must be considered before conclusion on obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person of ordinary skill is presumed to know all prior art determined reasonably relevant and to have ordinary creativity/common sense. Consider evidence of: (1) level of education and experience of persons actively working in the field as of the Cutoff Date, including inventors; (2) types of problems encountered in the art; (3) sophistication of the technology and rapidity of innovation as of the Cutoff Date. If parties agree on the level, instruct the jury accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor 4 — secondary considerations / other considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider objective indicia that may indicate obviousness or nonobviousness; no single factor is dispositive and must be considered with all evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant considerations include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not marketing), long-felt but unsolved need, failure of others to solve the problem, copying by others, unexpectedly superior results, praise or surprise by others, acceptance of licenses because of the merits. These factors are material only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the court determines admissibility and sufficiency of nexus before instructing the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field, as of the effective filing date, to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; lack of enablement renders a claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a question of law for the Court; the jury should be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if specific factual issues bearing on enablement must be decided. The Defendant bears the burden to establish it is highly probable the specification lacks enablement. Factors for undue experimentation include: quantity of experimentation and whether it involves only known techniques; amount of direction/guidance in the patent; presence/absence of working examples; nature of the invention; state of the prior art; relative skill of those in the art; predictability of the art; and breadth of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent specification must contain a written description of the product or method claimed; it must describe each limitation of a patent claim in sufficient detail to show the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description is a claim-by-claim inquiry. The requirement is satisfied if persons of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter, even if the exact claim language is not used and specific examples are not required. Consider: nature and scope of claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; existing knowledge in the field; and scope and content of the prior art. Written description is a question of fact — instruct the jury only if specific claims are challenged with sufficient evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If claims are found infringed and not invalid, the jury must determine damages adequate to compensate the plaintiff for the infringement; plaintiff must prove each element of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages aim to put the plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement. The award cannot be punitive or include interest, and cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. The jury should consider damages only if it finds at least one asserted claim both not invalid and infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — stipulated or disputed start date
rubrics_metrics.description: When calculating damages, the start date for the damages period may be stipulated by the parties or determined by the jury if disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate A: if parties agree, use stipulated date. Alternate B: if disputed, the date the plaintiff first notified the defendant of its claim for patent infringement is the start date; the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the defendant was put on notice as of the alleged date. (Methods of notice are enumerated in the full instruction.)
